### 1. execuTive summarY ##### InTRodUcTIon The lacklustre macro and demand environment has led us to pare our outlook back further, particularly for this year and 2013. We have also made some historical adjustments, mainly consisting of upward revisions to our global production numbers. For 2011, the net result of the adjustment caused our estimated deficit to fall from 256,000 tonnes to 162,000 tonnes. Ongoing weakness and uncertainty in the eurozone has been compounded by a slowdown in china and consumption prospects have been impacted not only in the mature economies, but in those of emerging markets too. Prices have retreated from the highs seen in February of this year, but have not yet challenged the lows of October 2011, even though market sentiment has grown more bearish, and the copper net short position (as published by the cFTc) is greater than at any time since 2009. During the first quarter of the year, the lme copper cash price ranged between $7,445/tonne and $8,765/tonne. in the second quarter, prices fell from a high of $8,703/ tonne in April, to a low of $7,220/tonne in June. During July and August, the copper price has traded in a lower and narrower range of $7,280-7,823/tonne. indeed, the average lme cash price for the first half of this year, at $8,107/tonne, is 14% lower than over the same period in 2011. china, being the key market for copper demand, has disappointed so

far this year, with a plethora of lessthan-sanguine data and consumption-indicator releases. chinese GDP growth fell to the lowest level in three years in the second quarter, of 7.6%, whilst chinese industrial production growth eased to 9.5% in June (from 11.9% in march). The growth in fixed asset investment also eased, although the decline here was less severe, with cumulative investment totalling 20.4% over JanuaryJune. more sector-specific chinese indicators also paint a downbeat picture for consumption. construction has continued to show signs of a slowdown, highlighted by the sharp declines in cumulative growth in floor space under construction and newly completed buildings. The white goods and appliance sectors have also weakened notably, as manufacturers react to ballooning levels of finished product inventory by scaling back operating rates. The power sector has showed signs of easing over the start of 2012, although the auto industry has more recently shown signs of recovery, following a dismal first quarter. in contrast to the slowdown in underlying consumption growth, apparent chinese usage continued to grow at a sensational pace, driven by a 73.6% rise in imports over the corresponding period. However, this vastly overstates the strength in underlying demand, and has been inflated by an increase in imports by the financial community (which continues to use copper as collateral for loans), and an increase in (overly-optimistic) bookings from traders and consumers. implicitly, this has led to the accumulation of significant levels of refined copper inventory within the country. The inventory build in both physical copper and in end-use appliances will need to be worked off before any meaningful additions to underlying consumption can take place in the country. We do, though, expect that measures to loosen monetary policy and to inject liquidity will help to improve the fundamental picture for china, but later than previously envisaged. Under our Base case, we expect a slowdown in world GDP growth this year. This will mainly be driven by the ongoing sovereign debt crisis in europe, weak industrial production in advanced economies and only limited scope for robust monetary easing. moreover, economic growth in developing countries is expected to slow further this year as a result of tight monetary policies implemented in a number of markets during 2011, together with poor external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in mature economies. Nevertheless, we expect the global economy to gradually improve in the latter years of our forecast. real global GDP growth is expected to fall to an annual average of 2.2% this year, before picking up to 2.6% and 3.5% in 2013 and 2014 respectively. improved investment appetite for metals, and copper in particular, with prices recovering in the fourth quarter and through the first half of next year. ##### economIc ASSUmpTIonS The stronger-than-expected economic performance in the eurozone in the first three months of the year may prove to be only temporary, as many eurozone economies continue to struggle amid elevated levels of unemployment, severe austerity measures and the sovereign debt crisis, which continues to intensify. looking across the Atlantic, the Us economy has continued to recover this year, although the pace at which it is doing so slowed considerably in the first quarter compared to the economic performance seen at end-2011. This confirms our view that recent improvements remain fragile and that the United states is still vulnerable to downside risks, including a deteriorating fiscal position, a weak housing market, elevated levels of unemployment and a further escalation of the eurozone crisis. chinese and indian policymakers have also been seen to be shifting towards measures supporting growth; china has implemented two interest rate cuts so far this year, with more seen likely. The overall OecD composite leading indicator remained static from February-may at 100.4, before dipping slightly to 100.3 in June. consumer confidence in the United states and european economies continued to slide. The ism purchasing managers’ index fell sharply in June to 49.7, from 53.5 in may, and did not recover in July. it is the first time that the index has fallen below 50 (indicating a contraction in Us factory activity) since July 2009. Also, chinese indicators continue to expose a slowdown in the country’s economy, especially the second quarter GDP release of 7.6% (from 8.1% in the first quarter), the slowest growth in three years. Under our more bullish scenario B, world GDP growth is projected to average 3.1% per annum over the forecast period. central

to this scenario are policies implemented by the Us government and the Federal reserve, in particular expansionary fiscal policies and ultra-loose monetary conditions. real GDP growth in the United states is therefore projected to average 2.5% between 2012 and 2014. This higher economic growth will, however, be achieved at the expense of higher inflation, which is forecast to rise from 2.7% in 2012 to 4.6% by the end of the forecast period (annual averages in each case). Under such circumstances, we would expect to see the Us dollar weaken from an annual average of $1.28/€ in 2012 to $1.35/€ by the end of the forecast. Under our more bearish scenario c, we expect to see a sluggish economic performance, particularly across the developed world, with growth rates remaining at historically low levels (especially for a post-recession phase of economic growth) throughout the forecast period. World GDP growth is, therefore, forecast to average around 1.9% per annum between 2012 and 2014. ##### The dollAR Having risen to a high of around $1.19/€ in June 2010, the dollar trended weaker through April 2011, hitting a low of over $1.49/€ in early may. eurozone issues caused this trend to reverse, with the dollar strengthening to almost $1.20/€ in July 2012, before easing to a recent level of around $1.25/€. looking ahead, given heightened market uncertainties, we remain of the view that the American currency will continue to benefit from investors’ flight to safe haven assets. The dollar is thus expected to average $1.26/€ this year, compared with $1.39/€ in 2011 and $1.33/€ in 2010. This has especially been the case in the past few years, and macroecono

mic events, perceptions and anticipations have largely outweighed fundamentals in driving price and volatility. Having had a net short stance through the fourth quarter of 2011 (according to the cFTc managed money category), a recovery in macro sentiment boosted copper prices into January of this year, as the market moved into a net long situation. This net long remained intact through much of the first half of 2012, and during most of this time the copper cash price traded in excess of $8,000/tonne. However, a turnaround in sentiment, as eurozone woes intensified and chinese growth fears began to mount, saw long liquidation push prices lower, and investors move into a net short position, greater than that of late 2011, but not to the extent reached in 2009. Given our assumption of liquidity injections in the United states, europe and china in the second half of this year, we assume that investors will regain confidence, which will also find an expression through a recovery in the copper price as they start to buy again. ##### conSUmpTIon Given the weaker-than-expected first half performance, coupled with our more bearish economic outlook, we have downwardly revised our demand forecasts in this report. Our latest projections show global demand growing by 2.4% this year (from 2.9% previously) to 20.287 million tonnes. This represents a reduction of 115,000 tonnes from our previous estimate. Our estimates show that copper demand growth continued to ease further over the start of 2012, with the global total over the first six months posting a gain of just 0.7% year-on-year. An intensification of concerns over the health of the global economy, in particular centering on worries over eurozone and chinese growth, has been a key driver of this trend. We do, though, continue to expect a recovery in copper demand growth over the second half of 2012, (cautiously) assuming an improvement in economic conditions based on further, broad, quantitative easing. china is expected to contribute to this trend, as an easing of monetary policy should begin to filter through to boost consumption in key end-use industries, whilst consumers should return to the market following a painful destocking phase that took place (at the downstream product s

tage) over the start of the year. in addition, the low base of the second half of 2011 should also help mature economy consumption growth return to positive territory. We expect 2012 to be the low point in terms of consumption growth rates over our forecast period, as a modest improvement in the economic environment facilitates an improvement in demand growth in 2013 to 3.5%. A continuation of such trends, as well as a weakening in copper prices, will also serve to add upward momentum to refined copper demand growth in the final year of our forecast period. A 3.7% rise is projected for 2014, taking total usage by the end of our forecast period to 21.767 million tonnes. ##### pRodUcTIon Although we have revised our supply-side numbers down slightly from the previous quarter, the general pattern of growth we are forecasting over the next three years remains relatively unchanged. Thereafter, we believe there will be a period of strong growth in mine supply, while remaining cautious that industry can deliver new production capability as planned. We estimate that global mine production reached 16.021 million tonnes in 2011. comparing that figure with historical statistics by the international copper study Group (icsG), suggests that over 2001-2011, mine production rose by a cumulative 17%. in our latest forecast, we expect copper mine production to grow by 2.2% this year, an increase of 345,000 tonnes on 2011 and a downward revision from our previous quarterly. looking forward into 2013 and 2014, global production capability is expected to increase significantly, with a number of new projects and expansions scheduled for commissioning. Our adjusted base case estimate is for growth of 4.3% a year over the next 2 years; this would bring total mine production to just over 17.8 million tonnes. From 2001 through to 2011, global refined copper production grew by 26% on a cumulative basis, to 19.658 million tonnes in the latter year. For 2012 as a whole, we forecast global refined copper production to grow by 3.1% to 20.271 million tonnes, 46,000 tonnes lower than our previous projection. We project that this expected acceleration in production growth over the second half will continue over the closing tw

o years of our forecast period, to 3.9% and 4.4% in 2013 and 2014, respectively, by which time output should have reached 21.976 million tonnes. A significant proportion of such increases are expected to come from the conventional smelting and refining route, in contrast to previous years when strong growth in sX-eW and/or secondary output have been the key drivers of gains. Thomson reuters GFms estimate the average total cash cost in 2011 at $2,865/tonne, up 16% on the previous year. The marginal cost of production, as defined by the 90th percentile of cash operating costs, at $4,410/tonne, was still significantly below the 2011 annual average copper price of $8,811/tonne. **6** 3-Year COPPer FOreCast - august 2012 confidential - not for distribution

This led us to make downward revisions in our last quarterly outlook, and we have done so again here. Offsetting some of the weaker consumption numbers are our slightly lowered expectations of global production growth, which continues to struggle, especially at the mine level. Whilst our historical consumption estimates have remained essentially unchanged, increased production numbers have loosened market balances slightly over the last couple of years. so, last year’s deficit now stands at 162,000 tonnes, compared to 256,000 tonnes previously. Given the weaker price performance so far this year and a macro environment that still presents headwinds to demand, as well as a fundamental picture which continues to suggest any pick-up will come later rather than sooner, our price forecasts for 2012 and 2013 have inevitably been lowered. On a quarterly basis, prices in the second quarter of this year were 4.0% lower on average than previously forecast, at $7,869/tonne and we expect a further fall to $7,500/tonne in the third quarter. orecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case, Scenario B and Scenario C. Under our **Base Case** , we expect a slowdown in world GDP growth this year. This will mainly be driven by the ongoing sovereign debt crisis in Europe, weak industrial production in advanced economies and only limited scope for robust monetary easing. Moreover, economic growth in developing countries is expected to slow further this year as a result of tight monetary policies implemented in a number of markets during 2011, together with poor external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in mature economies. Nevertheless, we expect the global economy to gradually improve in the latter years of our forecast. We view this as the most likely scenario, with a 45% probability. 

Under our more bullish **scenario B** , to which we assign a 30% probability, we expect a global economic recovery to materialise, with higher growth rates in both the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period. We assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve will implement further ultra-loose monetary and fiscal policies. We therefore expect to see the dollar weakening and US inflation rising during this period, with the US CPI reaching an annual average of 4.1% in 2014. Furthermore, we assume that under this scenario, the European Central Bank (ECB) will take additional easing measures with respect to tackling the Eurozone debt crisis. However, the slowdown in the global economy this year has led us to reduce the probability of Scenario B to 30%, from 40% in our earlier forecast. 

Under our more bearish **scenario C** , with a 25% probability (up from 15% in the previous report), we assume that no further easing measures will take place in the United States (or elsewhere), while a faster pace of fiscal consolidation emerges in Europe. As a result, world GDP growth is forecast to slow considerably this year and to remain sluggish over the remainder of the forecast period, particularly in the industrialised world. Under this scenario, therefore, we expect low levels of inflation, together with a stronger US dollar. 

The analysis below starts by describing the background to the current economic situation. We then discuss in more detail each of the three economic scenarios, with a particular focus on some key individual countries. 

The stronger-than-expected economic performance in the Eurozone in the first three months of the year may prove to be only temporary as many Eurozone economies continue to struggle amid elevated levels of unemployment, severe austerity measures and the sovereign debt crisis, which continues to intensify. Measures implemented by the EU leaders have so far done little to calm the markets and restore confidence across Europe. On the contrary, growing fears over the health of the financial sector in Spain have pushed its borrowing costs higher. Perhaps more importantly, yields

on Italian ten-year government bonds have also continued to rise. This suggests that the risk of contagion to the large Eurozone economies remains and that, given the high rates on Italian bonds, along with its deepening recession, it could be next to seek a bail-out. Looking across the Atlantic, the US economy has continued to recover this year, although the pace at which it is doing so slowed considerably in the first quarter compared to the economic performance seen at end-2011. This confirms our view that recent improvements remain fragile and that the United States is still vulnerable to downside risks, including a deteriorating fiscal position, a weak housing market, elevated levels of unemployment and a further escalation of the Eurozone crisis. In addition, despite a sluggish economic recovery, the Fed’s Chairman, Dr. Bernanke, indicated in his semi-annual congressional testimony that there was no imminent plan to launch another round of bond purchases. This has led to growing concerns that the country’s economy is going to stall in the coming months. Elsewhere, although economic performance in the major developing countries has remained relatively solid, the growth path has slowed as a result of a tightening of monetary and fiscal policies in 2011 and a weak recovery in demand from the advanced economies. A tighter than expected concentrate market during the first half of 2012, driven by disappointing mine production, is likely to ease through the second half of the year as key operations recover and new projects ramp up production. In recent history, copper mine production has tended to underachieve. The causes are well known; labour disputes, technical problems and an ongoing structural shortage in production capability, partly as a result of limited past investment. ###### MIne ProductIon 

We estimate that global mine production reached 16.021 million tonnes in 2011. Comparing that figure with historical statistics by the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) suggests that over 2001-2011, mine production rose by a cumulative 17%.  Throughout the period, concentrate output accounted for the bulk of global production. Nevertheless, the faster growth of solvent extraction electrowinning (SX-EW) production over the eleven years has seen the share of the latter increase from 18% in 2000 to 22% last year. 

Looking at the regional split of mine production, aside from the revival in African production, little has changed over the last decade.  The continent has seen the strongest growth over 2001-2011 and this has seen its share of global production rise from less than 4% in 2001 to almost 8% last year.  Elsewhere, Latin America remains the largest producing region, followed by Asia. 

The locations where copper is mined and those where it is smelted and refined into cathode can differ significantly. This is due to the fact that regions where copper is mined often do not enjoy the labour and energy cost advantages related to refining. More importantly, refining operations are often set up in key consumption centres. 

The above is clear when comparing the regional split of mined and refined production in 2011. For instance, although 45% of mine production was sourced in Latin America, less than a fourth of global refined production came from the region. In contrast, although around 20% of global mine production comes from Asia, the region accounted for 46% of global refined output. 

From 2001 through to 2011, global refined copper production grew by 26% on a cumulative basis, to 19.658 million tonnes in the latter year. The overwhelming bulk of the growth took place in Asia, with China undoubtedly the biggest force therein.  The region moved from accounting for 31% of production in 2001 to the aforementioned 46% share of global production last year. This came mostly at the expense of the Americas and, to a lesser extent, Europe and Oceania.
